sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.content:
"Fuck normal, I want magic."

El Woods is an immersive sustainable retail and cafe experience coming to West Denver, Colorado. We're creating a space where conscious consumption feels less like sacrifice and more like stepping into a woodland sanctuary—a place where shopping for secondhand fashion becomes a transformative experience rather than a transaction.

The concept brings together three integrated elements: Wardrobe Revival, our curated buy-sell-trade clothing operation; an Eco Cafe serving locally sourced coffee, tea, and baked goods; and The Collective, a rotating community space for local art, workshops, open mic nights, and events. Every element—from the living walls to the reclaimed wood fixtures—tells the same story of restoration and mindful living.

Proven Demand

We've already validated the El Woods concept through 3-5 pop-up events at local festivals and markets. Our average transaction of $50-$75 exceeded projections, confirming that customers will pay premium prices for curated, quality pieces. We're actively building inventory, growing our Instagram presence (@elwoods.revival), and in discussions with potential venue partners for an accelerated launch path.

The Opportunity

West Denver's suburban communities—Wheat Ridge, Golden, Lakewood, and Arvada—are underserved by curated sustainable retail. While Denver ranks fourth nationally for secondhand stores per capita, the market is concentrated in central neighborhoods. Our target customers, eco-conscious millennials earning $50K-$100K, currently drive to RiNo or Capitol Hill for the kind of experience we're building closer to home.

The timing is right. The global secondhand apparel market is projected to reach $350 billion by 2028, and Denver's cultural shift toward sustainability—evidenced by the 2022 Waste No More ordinance—signals growing demand for businesses that align profit with purpose.

Financial Overview

We project Year 1 revenue of $150,000-$180,000, growing to $220,000-$280,000 in Year 2. Clothing sales drive 65% of revenue with 60-70% gross margins, while the cafe contributes 30% and creates the daily foot traffic that pure retail competitors lack.

The Team

Morgan McIntosh brings 14+ years of retail, fashion, and customer experience expertise from MAC Cosmetics and Beauty Brands. Benjamin Tyson is a serial entrepreneur with multiple successful startup exits and was the youngest-ever Pipeline Entrepreneurial Fellowship member. Together, we combine creative vision with operational know-how.

The Vision: Beyond Retail

El Woods is designed to grow beyond a single location. Year 2 introduces El Woods Marketplace—an online platform connecting sustainable vendors, local artisans, and conscious consumers. Think Etsy meets sustainability, powered by our curated aesthetic and trusted brand. This platform leverages our physical presence into a scalable digital business while staying true to our mission.

The Ask

We're seeking $100,000-$125,000 to launch a 2,000-3,000 square foot location in West Denver. We're open to equity investment, convertible notes, revenue-based financing, or traditional loans—we're looking for partners who align with our mission and want to help build Denver's next great community destination.

sections.title: Company Description
sections.content:
El Woods is a social enterprise built on environmental stewardship and conscious consumerism. We're creating an immersive retail experience that transforms how people think about fashion and consumption—one where stepping through our doors feels like entering a forest sanctuary.

Structured as an LLC with a mission-driven approach, El Woods will occupy 2,000-3,000 square feet in West Denver—likely Wheat Ridge, Golden, Lakewood, or Arvada. These communities share our values but lack access to the kind of curated, experiential sustainable retail that thrives in central Denver.

Our Mission

We exist to combat fast fashion waste, raise awareness about deforestation, and create a community hub where conscious consumption meets immersive experience. This isn't just marketing language—it's embedded in every decision we make, from sourcing reclaimed wood for our fixtures to committing a portion of profits to wildfire prevention and forest restoration as we grow.

The Experience

Walk into El Woods and you're surrounded by living walls, abundant greenery, and the warm glow of natural light filtering through organic textures. The furniture is handmade by local artisans. The fixtures are reclaimed wood. Even the ambient sounds are designed to ground you in nature.

This isn't accidental. Every element tells the same story of restoration and mindful living. Customers don't just shop here—they step into a woodland sanctuary that reframes their relationship with consumption. The experience itself becomes part of the value we offer.

How We Make Money

El Woods generates revenue through five integrated streams. Clothing sales drive 65% of revenue through our buy-sell-trade model, where we purchase pre-loved items from customers at 30-40% of resale value and sell them at healthy margins. The Eco Cafe contributes 30%, serving locally sourced coffee, tea, and baked goods—and crucially, creating daily foot traffic that pure retail competitors can't match.

The remaining 5% comes from consignment partnerships with local sustainable designers, community events like workshops and open mic nights, and art sales commissions from our rotating gallery. These streams generate modest direct revenue but drive community engagement and customer loyalty that compounds over time.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.content:
The Fast Fashion Crisis

The fashion industry has a waste problem of staggering proportions. According to the EPA, 11.3 million tons of textile waste ends up in U.S. landfills annually—equivalent to 2,150 pieces discarded every second. The European Parliament reports that textile production is responsible for 20% of global clean water pollution, mainly from dyeing processes. A single cotton t-shirt requires 2,700 liters of water to produce (WWF)—enough drinking water for one person for 900 days.

Consumers increasingly understand this crisis. They want to make better choices. But the current alternatives aren't compelling enough to change behavior at scale.

The Thrift Store Gap

Traditional thrift stores—Goodwill, Salvation Army, ARC—serve an important purpose, but they're not designed to shift consumer culture. They're overwhelming, cluttered warehouses where finding something good feels like digging for treasure in a landfill. The experience is transactional, not transformational.

Even chain buy-sell-trade stores like Buffalo Exchange and Plato's Closet, while more curated, operate as basic resale outlets. They don't connect customers emotionally to the impact of their choices. They don't build community. They don't challenge the underlying overconsumption culture that created the problem in the first place.

Thrift stores are in need of a revival. Not just better merchandising—a fundamentally different approach that makes sustainable shopping feel like something people genuinely want to do, not something they settle for.

sections.title: Our Solution
sections.content:
El Woods transforms sustainable shopping from a transaction into a transformative experience. We're not just selling secondhand clothes—we're creating a space that makes people genuinely excited about conscious consumption.

Experience Over Transaction

The moment you walk into El Woods, you're transported. The forest-themed space—living walls, reclaimed wood, dappled natural light—shifts your mindset before you even look at the clothes. This isn't "cheap shopping." This is a lifestyle choice you feel good about.

Our selection is curated, not crammed. Quality over quantity. Each piece is chosen for style, condition, and story. Vintage finds share space with eco-conscious contemporary pieces and work from local sustainable designers. The hunt for something unique becomes part of the pleasure.

Connection and Community

Unlike transactional thrift stores, El Woods connects customers emotionally to the impact of their choices. Through thoughtful design, storytelling, and programming, we help people understand what sustainable fashion actually means—and feel the difference their choices make.

We're also building community. Open mic nights, art workshops, sustainability talks, book swaps—these events deepen awareness and create the kind of loyalty that transactional retail can't buy. Customers become advocates. The space becomes theirs.

Closing the Loop

Our buy-sell-trade model keeps clothing in circulation rather than heading to landfills. Customers bring us their pre-loved pieces, we pay them or offer store credit, and those items find new homes. It's a closed loop that generates inventory, drives repeat visits, and reinforces our mission with every transaction.

sections.title: Market Overview
sections.content:
Denver has emerged as one of America's most sustainability-conscious cities, creating fertile ground for El Woods' concept. The 2022 Waste No More ordinance—requiring mandatory composting and recycling for businesses—signals the kind of regulatory environment that rewards rather than burdens mission-driven companies like ours.

The numbers back this up. Denver ranks fourth highest per capita for vintage and secondhand stores in the United States. The culture is already here; people are already shopping sustainably. What's missing is an elevated, experiential destination that matches the values these consumers already hold.

Market Tailwinds

We're entering at the right time. The global secondhand apparel market is projected to reach $350 billion by 2028, growing nearly three times faster than traditional retail. Locally, Colorado's cafe and coffee industry is valued at $1.6 billion in 2025, with Denver cafes increasingly differentiating on sustainability—a trend that positions our Eco Cafe as relevant rather than niche.

The buy-sell-trade model specifically is experiencing steady growth as consumers seek both environmental responsibility and value. Platforms like Poshmark, Depop, and ThredUp have normalized secondhand shopping for younger consumers who previously associated thrift with stigma. These shoppers are now looking for physical experiences that match their digital habits—curated, aesthetic, shareable.

El Woods meets them where they're already headed.

sections.title: Target Market
sections.content:
El Woods targets the conscious millennial consumer—specifically those living in West Denver's growing suburban communities who currently lack convenient access to the kind of curated, experiential sustainable retail that thrives in central Denver neighborhoods.

Geographic Focus

Our target communities share strong demographics and values. Wheat Ridge (population 32,200, median income $87,598) and Arvada (population 123,000, median income $113,396) both skew toward the outdoor-oriented, environmentally conscious residents who align with our mission. Lakewood and Golden add growing populations with similar profiles.

These areas are currently underserved. Most curated sustainable retail is concentrated in RiNo, Capitol Hill, and South Broadway—a 20-30 minute drive for West Denver residents. We're bringing the experience to them.

Who They Are

Our ideal customer is eco-conscious without being preachy—someone who actively reduces their environmental impact but doesn't define themselves by activism alone. They're creative and artistic, valuing self-expression and unique style over fast fashion trends. They seek community and connection, showing up for local events and craving a sense of belonging in an increasingly fragmented world. Many are wellness-focused, prioritizing mental health, mindfulness, and balanced living.

Right now, these customers primarily shop at curated vintage boutiques when they can get to them, supplementing with Goodwill or ARC when they can't, and browsing Poshmark and Depop on their phones. They're willing to pay more for unique, sustainable pieces—they just need somewhere convenient that feels worth the trip.

The Curious Newcomer

Beyond our core customer, El Woods aims to attract people who are new to sustainable fashion entirely. For them, we provide an inviting, non-intimidating entry point—a space where conscious consumption feels aspirational rather than judgmental. Our immersive environment and educational programming shift perspective on consumption without lecturing.

This "gateway" approach expands our addressable market while fulfilling our mission to change behavior at scale.

sections.title: Unique Selling Proposition
sections.content:
El Woods isn't just another thrift store with better lighting. We're building something fundamentally different—a space where the experience itself is the product as much as the clothing or coffee.

Immersion Over Transaction

Walk into a typical thrift store and you're in a warehouse. Walk into El Woods and you're in a forest. The living walls, reclaimed wood, natural light, and ambient sounds create a restorative environment that shifts how customers feel before they even start shopping. That emotional grounding translates into longer visits, higher purchase rates, and the kind of word-of-mouth that marketing budgets can't buy.

One Cohesive Ecosystem

Most competitors do one thing: clothes, or coffee, or art. We integrate all three into a seamless experience. The cafe creates daily foot traffic that pure retail can't generate. The art gallery and events build community that transactional stores can't replicate. The clothing anchors it all with strong margins. Each element reinforces the others.

A Catalyst, Not Just a Store

Traditional resale operations move inventory. El Woods shifts behavior. Through our design, storytelling, events, and 10% giveback, we're actively changing how people think about consumption. Customers don't just buy from us—they join a movement. That kind of mission-driven positioning creates loyalty that competitors can't easily copy, because you can't fake authenticity.

sections.title: Products & Services
sections.content:
El Woods operates as three integrated businesses under one roof, each reinforcing the others: a curated clothing operation, an eco-conscious cafe, and a community collective.

Wardrobe Revival

The heart of El Woods is our buy-sell-trade clothing operation. We purchase pre-loved items directly from customers at 30-40% of resale value, curate them for quality and style, and sell them at accessible price points ranging from $15 basics to $100+ premium vintage pieces.

Beyond our own inventory, we showcase work from local sustainable designers and resellers through a consignment program. This creates variety without inventory risk while supporting the local maker community. The selection rotates constantly—there's always something new to discover, giving customers a reason to return.

Eco Cafe

The cafe serves locally sourced coffee from small-batch roasters, artisan teas, and baked goods from neighborhood bakeries. Drinks range from $4-7 for espresso and specialty options. Everything uses compostable packaging, and we'll operate as close to zero-waste as possible.

But the cafe isn't just a revenue stream—it's a traffic driver. Coffee customers come daily. Some browse and buy. Others just enjoy the space and tell their friends. Either way, they're experiencing our brand and building the habit of coming to El Woods.

The Collective

The collective is where community happens. We'll host regular programming—sustainability workshops, open mic nights, art walks, book swaps, and collaborative events with local organizations. A rotating gallery showcases local artists, with El Woods taking a modest commission on sales.

These activities generate some direct revenue, but their real value is deeper. They create belonging. They give customers reasons to return beyond shopping. They generate social content and word-of-mouth. And they attract the kind of values-aligned staff who want to work somewhere meaningful, not just clock in.

sections.title: Operations Plan
sections.content:
El Woods will operate six days a week, Tuesday through Sunday, with Monday reserved for behind-the-scenes work. We're open 10am-7pm Tuesday through Saturday and 11am-5pm on Sundays, with extended hours for special events as needed.

The Team

At launch, the founding team handles core operations. Morgan leads creative direction, merchandising, customer experience, and the buy-sell-trade process—the heartbeat of the clothing operation. Ben manages business operations, finances, marketing, and vendor relationships.

We'll hire 2-3 part-time staff at $15-$18/hour to cover barista duties and sales floor support. This keeps monthly staffing costs at $4,000-$6,000 while ensuring we have coverage during peak hours. As revenue grows, we'll add capacity accordingly.

A Day at El Woods

Mornings start with opening the cafe—fresh coffee brewing, pastry case stocked. While the espresso machine warms up, we refresh clothing displays and process new inventory from the previous day's buys. By 10am, doors open.

Afternoons are our peak hours. The lunch crowd comes for coffee and stays to browse. Buy-sell-trade appointments bring in new inventory. This is when the space comes alive—customers discovering pieces, lingering over lattes, artists dropping by to check on their work in the gallery.

Evenings wind down the retail side while setting up for any scheduled events. We reconcile sales, update inventory, and prep for the next day. On event nights—Thursdays for open mic, for example—the space transforms into something more: a gathering place, not just a store.

Inventory Flow

Clothing inventory comes from multiple channels: scheduled buy appointments where customers bring items for evaluation, walk-in trades, estate sales, and occasional wholesale vintage purchases. Everything gets quality-checked, cleaned or repaired if needed, photographed for social media, priced, and tagged. Items that don't sell within 60-90 days get marked down or donated—we keep the floor fresh.

Cafe inventory is simpler. Coffee arrives weekly from our local roaster partner. Baked goods come daily or every other day from a neighborhood bakery—fresh, local, no baking operation for us to manage. Compostable supplies get ordered bi-weekly.

Systems and Partners

We'll run on Square or Shopify POS, integrating retail and cafe transactions with real-time inventory tracking. Staff scheduling through Deputy or Homebase. QuickBooks for bookkeeping. Nothing exotic—proven tools that work.

Key vendor relationships include our coffee roaster (TBD), bakery partner (TBD), a local nursery for living wall maintenance, and waste services aligned with Denver's Waste No More requirements. These partnerships matter—they're part of our supply chain and part of our story.

Event Programming

Community programming runs on a regular calendar: open mic every Thursday, art walk and gallery rotations bi-weekly, monthly sustainability workshops and book swaps, and quarterly seasonal parties and artist showcases. This rhythm gives customers reasons to return and creates the social fabric that makes El Woods more than a store.

sections.title: Marketing Strategy
sections.content:
Our marketing strategy is grassroots by design. We're building awareness through organic channels, community connections, and word-of-mouth rather than paid advertising. This approach fits our budget, aligns with our brand values, and creates the kind of authentic engagement that paid media can't replicate.

"Fuck normal, I want magic."

That tagline captures our brand positioning. El Woods isn't just a store—it's an experience, a community hub, a catalyst for change in how people think about consumption. Every piece of marketing reinforces that identity.

Instagram as Home Base

Our primary channel is Instagram (@elwoods.revival), where we're already building presence before launch. Content focuses on behind-the-scenes buildout, featured items, sustainability education, artist spotlights, and event promotion. The aesthetic is moody forest vibes, natural lighting, earthy tones—consistent with the in-store experience.

We'll post 4-5 times weekly on feed with daily stories, prioritizing Reels for reach. TikTok and Pinterest may come later for expanded demographic reach and style inspiration content, but Instagram is where our target customer already lives.

Partnerships and Community

We're leveraging existing network connections—local artists, sustainable businesses, coffee roasters, bakeries, and environmental organizations. These relationships create natural co-marketing opportunities: rotating gallery exhibitions, cross-referrals, supplier partnerships with shared promotion, and collaborative events with nonprofits and community groups.

We'll also build an email list starting pre-launch, offering exclusive updates and early access to "founding members." A simple loyalty program rewards repeat customers and referrals. User-generated content—customers sharing their finds and tagging our location—extends our reach organically.

Launch Strategy

In the 8-12 weeks before opening, we'll tease the concept on Instagram with buildout progress, collect email signups, and announce key partnerships. Launch week brings a grand opening event with live music and local artist showcases, an exclusive early-access day for founding members, press outreach to Westword, 5280, and Denver Post, and invites to local influencers and micro-influencers.

Post-launch, marketing becomes ongoing community programming: weekly events drive consistent content and foot traffic, seasonal campaigns tie to sustainability themes, and customer spotlights keep the feed authentic and relatable.

Budget and Metrics

We're allocating $3,000-$5,000 for the launch campaign (event, PR, initial ads) and $500-$1,000 monthly ongoing. The emphasis is on organic and earned media—reinvesting in events that drive community and word-of-mouth rather than scaling ad spend.

Key metrics: Instagram follower growth and engagement rate, email list growth, event attendance, customer acquisition cost, repeat customer rate, and referral tracking. These tell us whether our grassroots approach is working.

sections.title: Management Team
sections.content:
El Woods is led by a husband-and-wife founding team whose skills complement each other: Morgan brings retail, fashion, and customer experience expertise; Ben brings entrepreneurial and operational know-how. Together, we cover the creative and business sides of building something new—and we both bring food service management experience directly relevant to the cafe operation.

Morgan McIntosh | Founder & Creative Director

Morgan has spent over 14 years in retail, fashion, and customer experience. At MAC Cosmetics (2010-2015), she worked as a Makeup Artist & Product Specialist across multiple locations, leading teams, training staff, and educating customers on product trends. At Beauty Brands, she managed the makeup department as Lead Makeup Artist & Beauty Specialist, driving sales and ensuring customer service excellence.

Critically for El Woods' cafe component, Morgan also brings restaurant management experience from a major restaurant chain, understanding the operational demands of food service from the inside.

Since 2010, Morgan has worked independently as a fashion stylist, makeup artist, and consultant for weddings, photo shoots, and special events. Her editorial work includes beauty direction for commercial and avant-garde photoshoots.

What Morgan brings: Customer experience design, visual merchandising, trend awareness, team leadership, restaurant operations experience, and deep understanding of retail at the ground level.

Benjamin Tyson | Co-Founder & Business Operations

Ben is a serial entrepreneur and technologist with a track record of founding and scaling ventures. He was selected as the youngest-ever member of the Pipeline Entrepreneurial Fellowship for pioneering work on core technology behind Google Earth. He founded Beta Killers, a tech prototyping laboratory, and has successfully founded and exited multiple startups across sectors including laser technology and hemp science.

Directly relevant to El Woods: Ben served as manager at a 4-star restaurant, handling both front-of-house and back-of-house operations—experience that directly applies to our cafe. He also owns and operates a successful laser engraving studio with global online sales, demonstrating expertise in e-commerce and product sales that will inform our future marketplace expansion.

What Ben brings: Business development, startup operations, financial planning, restaurant management (FOH/BOH), e-commerce expertise, and experience scaling ventures from idea to exit.

Why This Partnership Works

Morgan drives the brand experience—the look, feel, and emotional connection that makes El Woods special. Ben drives the business—operations, growth strategy, and the mechanics of building a sustainable company. Both bring food service experience that addresses a common concern for retail-plus-cafe concepts.

As a married couple, we share not just a business vision but a life commitment. The ownership structure is straightforward, and our incentives are fully aligned. We've bet on each other—and we're betting on El Woods together.

Commitment

Morgan will be full-time dedicated to El Woods operations from launch. Ben will contribute part-time initially while transitioning from his current business, moving to full-time as the business scales.

sections.title: Funding Request
sections.content:
We're seeking $100,000-$125,000 to launch El Woods. The founders are committing $5,000-$10,000 of personal capital, and we're looking for partners who share our vision and want to help build something meaningful.

Funding Sought

$100,000 - $125,000
Total raise target

Founder Investment

$5,000 - $10,000
Personal capital committed

Use of Funds

100%
Launch & operations

Where the Money Goes

The largest allocation—about 27%—goes toward creating the immersive forest environment that makes El Woods distinctive. This isn't decorating; it's building our core product experience. Cafe equipment takes another 16%, and lease deposits require 14% upfront. We're holding 15% as working capital to weather the early months before revenue ramps.

CategoryAmount%
Build-out & Forest Immersion Design$30,00027%
Cafe Equipment & Setup$18,00016%
Lease & Deposits$15,00014%
Initial Inventory$12,00011%
Furniture, Fixtures & Technology$10,0009%
Marketing & Launch$5,0005%
Licenses, Permits & Legal$3,0003%
Working Capital Reserve$17,00015%
TOTAL$110,000100%

How We're Structuring This

We're open to different investment structures depending on what works for our partners. Equity investment with profit-sharing gives investors ownership in what we're building. Convertible notes provide debt that converts to equity at a future valuation. Revenue-based financing lets us repay as a percentage of sales. Traditional loans or SBA financing are also on the table.

We're exploring multiple funding sources: angel investors who care about sustainability and retail, SBA 7(a) loans and microloans, Community Development Financial Institutions focused on local economic development, sustainability-focused grants for social enterprises, and potentially a community crowdfunding campaign.

The Return

We expect to hit break-even between months 8 and 12, with Year 1 revenue of $150,000-$180,000 growing to $220,000-$280,000 in Year 2. Gross margins are strong: 60-70% on clothing, 65-75% on cafe. These aren't aspirational numbers—they're based on comparable businesses and conservative traffic assumptions.

Exit Scenarios

We're building El Woods to be a lasting, profitable business—not a quick flip. That said, we've considered how investors might realize returns:

  • Profit Distributions: Once profitable, we anticipate distributing a portion of annual profits to investors on a pro-rata basis. This is our primary return mechanism.
  • Founder Buyout: After Year 3-5, we may offer to buy out investor positions at an agreed-upon multiple, allowing founders to consolidate ownership as the business matures.
  • Strategic Acquisition: If El Woods demonstrates the model works, larger sustainable retail or hospitality companies may find value in acquiring the brand and expanding it regionally.

The specific structure will depend on the investment vehicle and partner preferences—we're flexible on terms that align everyone's interests.

Why This Matters

The secondhand apparel market is projected to reach $350 billion globally by 2028. El Woods is positioned to capture a slice of that growth in an underserved market (West Denver) with a differentiated concept (immersive retail + cafe + community) that no competitor currently offers.

We have an experienced team with complementary skills, a mission-driven model that builds genuine customer loyalty, and multiple revenue streams that diversify risk. For investors aligned with sustainability and conscious consumerism, El Woods offers exposure to a movement, not just a business.

The Bigger Vision: El Woods Marketplace

Beyond the physical store, we're developing plans for an El Woods online marketplace—think Etsy for thrifted, vintage, and eco-conscious goods. This platform would:

  • Sell our own inventory to a national audience
  • Host other sustainable sellers and curators
  • Create an entirely separate revenue stream independent of physical location
  • Position El Woods as a brand and platform, not just a store

This is a Year 2+ initiative, but it represents significant upside beyond our base projections and a path to scaling without geographic constraints.

sections.title: Social & Environmental Mission
sections.content:
El Woods exists at the intersection of commerce and cause. We're building a profitable business, but profit isn't the only point. Our model is designed to create measurable positive impact on the environment and community—not as marketing, but as core to who we are.

"We believe business can be a force for good—and that magic happens when profit and purpose align."

Our Approach to Impact

We believe in building a sustainable giving model—one that grows with the business rather than jeopardizing it. Our approach prioritizes operational impact first (the daily environmental benefit of what we do), with charitable giving ramping up as the business reaches profitability.

Year 1: Impact Through Operations

In our first year, our primary environmental impact comes from the business itself. Every piece of clothing we sell is one diverted from a landfill. Every item we buy from a customer stays in circulation. This isn't a donation line item—it's built into every transaction.

Year 1 Operational Impact GoalsTarget
Clothing items resold (diverted from landfill)3,000+
Pounds of textiles diverted2,500+ lbs
Water saved (vs. new production)8+ million liters

The cafe runs on compostable cups, lids, and napkins with a full composting program. Retail uses reusable bags and recycled paper. The build-out prioritizes reclaimed wood and upcycled materials. We're aligned with Denver's Waste No More ordinance—not because we have to, but because it's who we are.

Year 2+: The Giveback Pledge

Once El Woods reaches sustainable profitability, we commit to donating 5-10% of net proceeds to environmental causes. We're being intentional about this timeline—better to build a strong foundation and give consistently for decades than to overcommit early and scale back.

Target Giveback

5-10%
of net proceeds (Year 2+)

Year 2 Goal

$10,000+
in environmental donations

Year 3 Goal

$20,000+
in environmental donations

Where It Goes

Our giving focuses on two areas: wildfire prevention and recovery and deforestation awareness. Colorado has experienced devastating wildfires in recent years—the Marshall Fire, the Cameron Peak Fire, countless others. This cause is local and personal. We'll support prevention programs, forest restoration initiatives, firefighter and first responder organizations, and community recovery efforts.

On deforestation, we'll partner with reforestation organizations, host educational programming, and support tree-planting initiatives. The forest theme of El Woods isn't just aesthetic—it's a reminder of what we're fighting for.

Community Impact

El Woods supports local artists and sustainable designers. Emerging artists get free gallery space with 70-80% of sales going directly to them. Sustainable designers access our consignment program for exposure and sales. We'll host regular showcases and collaborative events featuring sustainable fashion.

Educational programming—upcycling workshops, sustainable living talks, partnerships with youth environmental organizations—extends our impact beyond transactions. We're not just selling clothes; we're building a community around environmental stewardship.

Accountability

We'll track and report on key impact metrics annually: dollars donated, clothing items diverted, artists supported, events hosted, waste reduction achieved. Transparency builds trust, and we want our customers and stakeholders to see exactly where their money goes.

Why This Matters for the Business

This isn't just altruism—it's good business. Our target customers care about where their money goes. A sustainable giving model differentiates us from competitors, builds customer loyalty, creates PR opportunities, and attracts employees who want to work somewhere meaningful. And honestly? It aligns with our personal values as founders. We wouldn't build it any other way.

sections.title: Risk Analysis
sections.content:
Risk Assessment & Mitigation

A realistic assessment of key risks and strategies to address them.

1. Market Risks

RiskMitigation
Economic downturn reduces discretionary spendingSecondhand clothing is recession-resistant; positioned as affordable alternative to new retail
Slower-than-expected customer adoptionPre-launch community building; leverage existing network; events drive foot traffic
West Denver location lacks foot trafficDestination concept - customers come specifically for El Woods experience; cafe as daily draw

2. Operational Risks

RiskMitigation
Difficulty sourcing quality inventoryMultiple sourcing channels (buy appointments, trades, estate sales, wholesale); build buy-seller relationships
Staff turnover in tight labor marketCompetitive wages; mission-driven culture attracts aligned employees; flexible scheduling
Cafe operations complexitySimplified menu; partnership with bakery (not in-house baking); trained barista staff

3. Financial Risks

RiskMitigation
Cash flow challenges in early monthsWorking capital reserve (3+ months); conservative revenue projections; lean operations
Build-out costs exceed budgetDetailed contractor quotes; phased build-out if needed; DIY elements where possible
Unable to secure fundingMultiple funding source approach; scaled-down launch option; continue exploring partnerships

4. Competitive Risks

RiskMitigation
Competitors copy the conceptFirst-mover advantage in West Denver; deep community roots difficult to replicate; authentic brand
Online resale platforms growEl Woods offers experiential value that online can't match; community events create loyalty
New thrift stores enter marketDifferentiated positioning (immersive experience vs. bargain hunting); premium curation

5. External Risks

RiskMitigation
Lease issues or rent increasesNegotiate multi-year lease with fixed increases; build landlord relationship
Supply chain disruptionsMultiple vendor relationships; local sourcing reduces dependency on distant suppliers

Risk Summary

Overall risk level: Moderate

El Woods operates in a growing market (sustainable fashion) with differentiated positioning and an experienced team. Primary risks center on execution and cash flow management in the early months, which are addressed through adequate capitalization and conservative planning.
